name: Erik Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play drums for a dance band, record percussion for local adverts and teach private beginners at a rented studio. I have a music degree, but most days I earn my fee by arriving early enough to tune a kit nobody else touched.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what takes planning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the beat that gets a shy couple dancing. My partner works as a school nurse, and we trade the two children’s pickups around band nights and the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that faster invoices are useful, but a computer cannot watch a crowded dance floor for me. I would still call the tempo from behind the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have three months of household expenses saved, and my partner’s school-nurse pay is steady. Festival dates are uneven already, so I cannot treat the mortgage as somebody else’s worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep Friday dance sets and my six beginner pupils this season. I already use AI daily to make practice lists, then I play the patterns myself before sending them to a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the usual gaps between bookings. In this picture AI itself does not take away a paid night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a booking last fall through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The autumn fair cancelled on a rainy morning and still paid the deposit we had written down. I would ask for the same deposit clause before next year’s fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your pupils hear first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They hear me count four steady beats before I touch a fill. Fast hands are no use if the dancers lose their feet.

say: I would welcome **faster invoices** while keeping live tempo in the band.
I would request a **written deposit clause** for fair bookings.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and school-nurse income cover ordinary short gaps.
Uneven **festival dates** still matter to the mortgage.
do: Keep **Friday dance sets** and six private drum pupils this season.
Ask for a **written fair deposit** before next year’s booking.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about existing gaps between paid nights.
S0.quote: Fast hands are no use if the dancers lose their feet.
fieldNote: His **three-month reserve** makes ordinary booking gaps matter despite a steady second earner.
Daily **AI practice lists** are existing use, checked by playing before children receive them.

steps.text: Keep Friday dance-band sets and six private drum pupils this season
Request written fair deposit clause before next year’s booking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band leader that software may write jingles and manage bookings, so we need written fees for the live sets. I would ask which rehearsal nights are actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert percussion I record is about a quarter of my good-month pay, and cheaper tracks could take those calls. The dance band has customers now, but fewer live dates would hurt the household too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for three months of paid band dates and an engineer-led session on the studio’s new stem-cleaning tool, which cleans separate recorded drum parts. In the first year I would test it only on my own drum take with the engineer’s approval, compare every cleaned beat to the original, and stop if the rhythm changes or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about those recording fees. I can learn a new control, but I cannot make an advertiser buy a drummer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a pupil’s recording through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would leave pupils’ recordings alone without their consent and a storage rule. My first test would be a take I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the band offers only one paid date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my existing pupils and ask about an advertised paid house-band opening nearby. I would apply only if its written net fee after travel beats the lost band pay and the call time fits pickup.

I would ask for **engineer-led training** on the new cleaner.
think: My **advert percussion** could lose a quarter of good-month pay.
Fewer **live dance dates** would further strain the household.
do: Request three months of **paid dates** from the band leader next month.
Test the **stem cleaner** after engineer approval on my own take; compare beats and stop on rhythm or studio-boundary failure.
Seek a **posted house-band opening** if dates fall, only with better written net pay and pickup fit.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording fees and possible lost live dates.
S1.quote: I can learn a new control, but I cannot make an advertiser buy a drummer.
fieldNote: His **new cleaner trial** needs engineer approval, his own recording, beat comparison and a studio-boundary stop.
A different **band seat** requires a posted paid opening, better net fees after travel and pickup fit.

steps.text: Test stem cleaner after engineer approval on own take; compare beats, stop on rhythm error/leakage
Keep six private drum pupils while requesting three months of paid band dates
Apply for posted paid house-band seat if dates fall, net pay improves and pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2028 could make advert tracks without my drum kit. I would ask the leader to sign the live dates and deposits while clubs still book us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert sessions to dry up in 2028 and some clubs to use generated backing tracks. Hands-on playing robots come around 2031, three years later. A quarter of my pay can disappear before a robot lifts a stick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total my advert invoices and get a written band calendar. If 2028 cuts paid band nights too, I would apply for a posted school percussion tutor job only if my music degree qualifies, its written net pay after travel beats the lost gigs and the hours fit pickup; I would keep pupils and band calls until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because I expect the lost adverts and some band dates together to take a large share of my own income. Three months saved will not cover a long search alongside a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new recording gear to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep two months of expenses untouched instead of borrowing for a new kit. I need a paying booking before spending on gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school post sounds promising but is not advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing and teaching. A friend’s hint is not a vacancy or a written pay offer.

say: I would ask for **signed live dates** and deposits before clubs change plans.
I would look for a **posted tutor vacancy** if paid band nights fall.
think: My **advert sessions** likely end in 2028 before 2031 playing robots.

do: Total **advert invoices** and request a signed band calendar now.
If 2028 band dates fall, apply for a **posted tutor job** only if qualified, net pay beats lost gigs and pickup fits.
Keep **pupils and band calls** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected large losses and a three-month reserve.
S2.quote: A quarter of my pay can disappear before a robot lifts a stick.
fieldNote: He expects **2028 recording losses** and some band cuts before physical robots around 2031.
A school **tutor move** needs a posted vacancy, degree eligibility, written net improvement, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Apply after 2028 band cuts for posted tutor role if qualified, written net-after-travel improves, pickup fits
Keep drum pupils and band calls until suitable written school offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dance band that five years until AGI by 2031 lets us build something people can join in person. I would offer a paid family rhythm class rather than another free show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert calls may end by 2031, but a class could replace a slice if families pay. Robots that can play arrive around 2034; a live class still needs a safe room and someone watching the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the community centre for a Saturday room after our children’s pickup and take deposits only if six families prepay enough to cover the room, safe loan drums and my teaching fee. In the first year after 2031 I would run the class again only if six paid places still cover the room and my teaching fee, the room remains available, instruments pass inspection and pickup still works; I would keep my current pupils meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the class pays for my time. Five years gives me a chance to test a paid rhythm class without borrowing against the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an old drum has a loose rim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have the centre check every loan drum before a child touches it. If one fails, I would remove it from the class rather than hide the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only three families pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three fees will not cover the room or a teaching wage. I would refund them and keep the existing lessons instead of running a loss-making class.

Repeat the **paid class** after 2031 only with six prepayments covering room and teaching, available room, inspected drums and pickup.
Keep **existing drum pupils** if the class cannot cover costs.
feel: I feel **anxious** until a class covers my own time.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a chance to test a paid rhythm class without borrowing against the house.
fieldNote: His class requires **six prepaid places** covering a room, safe drums and his own fee.
Renewal after 2031 still needs **room availability**, inspected drums and child pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that a decade until AGI by 2036 is time to build skills and earn the fee honestly. A full dance floor means little if the drummer is paid in promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert sessions could end by 2036 and live bands may face robots around 2039. Our three-month reserve and the mortgage mean I cannot wait until the final club closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would save ten percent of each paid advert session after the mortgage and food, aiming for six months and keeping two untouched if sessions stop. I would take a funded evening sound-tech certificate only if the course has a real place and my partner can cover pickup without losing paid shifts; in the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted sound-desk opening only if I qualify, written net pay after travel beats lost gigs and pickup fits; I would keep band and pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing recording and later stage fees. A funded course and a real job opening give me a route, but neither is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an unfunded course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not spend the mortgage reserve on tuition. If funding or pickup fails, I would keep playing and wait for another intake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if advert sessions end before six months are saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save spare pupil fees only after essentials are paid. Two months of household expenses would stay untouched while I look for posted work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert sessions and club nights might fall before I have a second paid route. Signed band dates, a real school vacancy and pickup that works would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the owner pays the last band member when a wedding runs late. I count the final bus home as part of a paid night.

headlineQuote: I count the final bus home as part of a paid night.
portrait: At **43**, Erik is an experienced drummer with a music degree, two children, a mortgage and three months saved.
His partner’s **school-nurse pay** steadies bills while dance-band nights and advert percussion supply typical musician earnings.
He uses **AI daily**, but tests a new stem cleaner only on his own take with engineer approval and listening checks.
He plans a **paid rhythm class** with six prepaid places, inspected drums, an available room and a teaching wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase advert sessions and reduce paid band nights before a second route pays.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed band dates**, a real school tutor vacancy and workable pickup would give Erik options.
